answers.text: Lock the output to three fixed lines in a set order so it can't drift between runs. Each line gets a precise definition, so there's no ambiguity about what goes where. Build in an explicit fallback for a missing field, not a blank line or a guessed number.
Specify the list structure exactly: one line per call, fixed fields, a follow-up flag on each. Specify the count is calculated from the flagged rows themselves, so two runs match.

The timing in this note doesn't reconcile with itself. Starting 8am for a six-hour job finishes around 2pm on the 22nd itself, not the 23rd as stated. It comes down to the finish date disagreeing with its own arithmetic — six hours doesn't reach the next day.
Recalculating, 96 to 118 comes out at about 23%, not the stated 20%. The on-time rate itself is consistent: 9 late out of 118 is roughly 92%, matching what's stated.

Output 2 is the one to approve, since the number is derived, not asserted. Output 1 leaves out the two figures behind the percentage — total tickets and SLA closures. The 88% could still be correct — it's just unverifiable as written, without re-counting.

I'd send Email 2 without further checking — it cites the volume figures and PO log. Email 1 asserts 'a better rate' with no reference — no volume figures, no PO log. That doesn't make Email 1 wrong — once backed by the same volume figures, it's just as sendable.

I'd treat the rates and retainer cap as sensitive by default — redact or confirm the tool's vetted first. Because the NDA clause names both the client and us, it gets the same caution as the pricing. The general scope of service carries little risk and can go in unredacted.

The check is a fixed cross-cast — recalculate from the warehouse system, set against the drafted summary. It's placed immediately before the summary leaves my hands, not folded loosely into the month.
An error at extraction doesn't stay contained; it propagates through the PO match and approval note.
